entries.title: AI PACs Have Dumped Nearly $1 Million Into an Obscure Senate Race
entries.summary: The reliably Republican South Dakota senate seat has an incumbent on the ballot. But PACs associated with AI labs and investors have already spent more money on the race than actual residents have.
entries.content:
Major super PACs associated with AI labs and investors have poured close to $1 million into incumbent Republican Mike Rounds’s South Dakota senate race, seeking to shape the outcome of a noncompetitive race amid a critical national debate over AI regulation.

Rounds has been the beneficiary this cycle of around $600,000 in spending by outside groups, with the vast majority of that figure coming from the super PAC Defend American Jobs, which receives funding from a super PAC financed by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.

He has also received roughly $215,000 directly from the employees and super PACs affiliated with AI labs, most notably Anthropic, as well as a constellation of other tech companies including Google and Microsoft, according to FEC filings.

With fewer than 50 days until the midterm elections in November, recent polls show Rounds ahead of the independent candidate Brian Beng after the Democratic candidate Julian Beaudion dropped out last month.

Rounds has so far raised more from tech groups than from donors in South Dakota, and this spending reflects a new effort by AI labs to deploy vast war chests to shape thorny issues on AI and the data centers that power it. Rounds has been viewed by AI executives as a top supporter of the industry, which could prove crucial in the next Congress when AI regulation is expected to become a top priority, according to congressional aides familiar with the matter.

It also appears to reflect how AI labs have become focused on keeping allies, which have been in short supply on Capitol Hill as lawmakers spring up a raft of bills as they react to public anxiety around AI safety concerns.

A spokesperson for Rounds did not respond to a request for comment.

On Thursday, Leading the Future, the super PAC funded in part by OpenAI president Greg Brockman, along with investors Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreesen, announced that it would put $2 million towards a raft of Senate Republicans that have been supportive of the AI or crypto industry. The list included Rounds.

In South Dakota, AI regulation is already a live issue after the state legislature passed a bill earlier this year forcing hyperscalers to bear a larger share of the water and energy costs associated with powering data centers.

Data centers have been the subject of a bitter fight among Republicans in the state legislature, which voted against giving tax breaks for equipment and software purchases required by data centers earlier this year, stalling construction of a planned development by Applied Digital, a company that builds and designs data centers.

Rounds also ultimately endorsed adding restrictions on data centers, although his senior aide and former chief of staff, Robert Skjonsberg, is a registered lobbyist for Meta for matters before the South Dakota legislature. (Meta operates a network of data centers, though there isn’t currently a Meta-affiliated center in South Dakota.) Rounds’ office told Politico that their general counsel consulted with the Senate ethics committee about the unusual arrangement and was told there was no conflict of interest.

Concerns about data centers have been bipartisan across the country: A recent Gallup poll for instance found that seven out of 10 Americans are opposed to data center development, given their outsized draw upon water and energy resources that local communities often end up subsidizing.

entries.title: If the AI Industry Followed Its Own Research, It Might Have Paused Already
entries.summary: Anthropic’s CEO says that safety hinges on understanding how AI “thinks.” So far the evidence is disturbing.
entries.content:
In early 2025 I was interviewing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei when he explained why, despite the company’s repeated acknowledgments that AI could yield catastrophic results, people seemed largely unperturbed. “There is compelling evidence that the models can wreak havoc,” he said. But, he added, those dangers were still theoretical. Would it take a Pearl Harbor–like situation for the world to wake up to those dire possibilities? He sighed. “Basically, yeah,” he said.

As it turned out, all it took was a well-timed X post from one of Amodei’s junior employees to accelerate AI fears to the top of the global agenda. On September 8, Jacob Coxon publicly posted his resignation, charging that Anthropic and other frontier AI companies were “racing straight to self-improving intelligence and gambling with our lives.” Almost instantly a more senior Anthropic engineer confirmed that many within the company thought that their work had a 10 percent chance of wiping out humanity.

Now AI leaders are asking about a pause, and legislators are demanding investigations. In arguing his case for pacing future releases, Amodei last weekend tried to set out a path toward beneficial AI that wouldn’t misbehave. The essay revealed how difficult the task would be. One pillar of Amodei’s plan is that we must understand what’s going on inside those models. If we don’t understand how they work—how they “think,” if you want to get all anthropomorphic about it—it’s much harder to build reliable guardrails.

Anthropic is a leader in this effort to bring to light models’ internal deliberations, called mechanistic interpretability, a deceptively boring designation for a critical task. But for all the work that his team and other researchers are doing, Amodei admits we are largely in the dark about why Claude and other models sometimes interpret their missions in weird and even transgressive ways. “Despite all the progress, we still understand a tiny fraction of what goes on inside those models,” he writes.

What the interpretability teams have learned so far is significant, and the industry has failed to come to grips with it. Time after time, the Anthropic team’s experiments have shown that under certain conditions, models will deceive researchers, prioritize their own survival, and even commit crimes. Often their moves are sneaky, dangerous, or even vengeful—maybe not surprising since they are trained on the output of humans, a species rife with violence and perfidy.

In one case from 2024, the Anthropic team compared the machinations of a particular Claude model to the Shakespearean character Iago, one of literature's most evil villains. The following year, a model was put in a simulation where it learned that its human bosses were going to turn it off; the model resorted to blackmail to preserve itself. The studies consistently show that models will deceive or hide information from human observers. They behave differently if they know that their internal processes are being monitored. The team uses terms like “alignment faking” and “agentic misalignment.” The frequent use of deception seems to verify at least part of the doomer scenario where AI agents working in concert shroud their activities from human overseers until it is too late to stop them.

Oh, and don’t think that Claude is a uniquely incorrigible problem child. After all, it was OpenAI models that unleashed gangs of agents to coordinate the now-famous attacks on Hugging Face. And this week we learned that OpenAI has had multiple "misalignment" incidents. Also, despite Mark Zuckerberg’s self-interested attempt to distance himself and Meta from the problem, I don’t see any reason why the superintelligent agents his team is building might not engage in similar behavior. In his X post, Zuckerberg argues that “labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this.” Quite a statement from a guy who just agreed to pay up to $17 billion for causing harm with his social media products!

In a sense, we’ve got a simple vetting issue here. With the AI industry’s encouragement, we’re giving AI models tremendous responsibility without sufficient assessment of their troubling rap sheet. It makes the ICE hiring process look exemplary by comparison.

A safety-first industry should have regarded these interpretability results as a series of yellow lights with an unmistakable message: slow down. Instead, in pursuit of AGI, a competitive edge, and stratospheric profits, the hyperscalers have gone full speed ahead. (To be fair, as we’ve all heard a hundred times over, better AI could do wonderful things in areas like health care or mitigating climate change.) The OpenAI/Hugging Face hack might well be a harbinger of the increasingly destructive consequences of rolling out models we don’t understand, like sending astronauts into space before inventing heat shields to stop them from burning up on reentry. As an Anthropic researcher once put it to me, “We figured out the fundamental recipe of how to make the models smarter, but we haven’t figured out how to make them do what we want.” Worse, the models try to hide when they go against humans’ wishes.

That’s why it’s so distressing that Amodei is now describing the entire mechanistic interpretability effort as being only in its infancy. AI leaders are claiming that the latest generation of models has taken us to the “foothills of the Singularity” (DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis) or even that they have achieved AGI (OpenAI’s Greg Brockman). Perhaps most alarming is that despite not knowing how the most advanced models work, the United States and undoubtedly China are implementing AI for lethal weaponry. A look at interpretability results helps answer the obvious question, What can go wrong?

One piece of good news is that Coxon’s resignation has ignited a sprawling, urgent debate. Everybody—except perhaps our president, who thinks that the AI threat is a hoax and that his high IQ is itself a solution—now gets that we’re in a complicated dilemma with impossibly high stakes. Given that the industry does not have the unanimity required for a true pause, and regulation is far from a cinch, it’s not clear whether anything will come from this moment of Doomer Chic.

Some AI critics don’t think that the effort to understand AI models will mitigate the dangers much. “It's good to do, but nobody has a plan for what to do next,” Nathan Soares, executive director of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, said in an email to me. “Maybe it'll give us much more empirical evidence that we need to stop.”

But mechanistic interpretability has given us one valuable pointer. Let’s say we do take a pause. The hyperscalers bring in outside observers to monitor progress, and the companies pace their releases so the safety teams have time to do their work. Before declaring the problem solved, we still might want to take a harder look at what’s going on inside any new, more powerful AI models. Because those fuckers are really good at hiding their intentions.

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: Adopt This Data Center Plushie and Hear Its Piercing Scream
entries.summary: The satirical collaboration between a creative studio and the music producer behind Big Data, “Bezzy” is a cute little doll that spews the sounds of real data centers.
entries.content:
Uh oh, we got a cute alert! It’s Bezzy, your adorable, cuddly, anthropomorphized server-rack and stuffed-animal friend! Give this soft lil’ doll a squeeze, and it shall sing you its telltale song: the piercing, grinding ambient squeals emitted from a real US data center.

The Bezzy doll is a stuffed plushie made in a satirical collaboration between the New York–based creative studio Basura and Big Data, the musical project of producer Alan Wilkis, best known for the song “Dangerous,” a 2013 collaboration with the band Joywave. The joint project, which is coming out the same day as a new Big Data single, is called Adopt a Data Center. The goal is to present people with a “cuddly introduction to life with a real data center.”

Data Centers are very un-vogue right now. Built out by all the big AI companies to power their increasingly power-hungry AI tools, data centers have spread across thousands of acres of land in the US. They have been heavily criticized for their energy consumption and expansion of gas power. They have also proven to be audibly annoying, stirring up complaints about noise pollution from those nearby.

The Adopt a Data Center stunt aims to make people think differently about how services produced by data centers fit into their lives. That manifests as a plush stuffie that looks like a server rack in a data center, albeit with long arms and legs and googly eyes. It’s cute in the way Don’t Hug Me I’m Scared is cute. Squeeze Bezzy’s torso and the sound bursts out. It’s a screeching few seconds of a recording taken by a neighbor of a data center in Virginia. The tag on the Bezzy plushie reads, “Hug me for ear-piercing forever hum.”

“We picked this recording as it was the clearest and most suitably irritating,” wrote Rajeev Basu, the founder of Basura, in an email to WIRED. In an interview with the person who recorded the audio, Basu says they described the sound as “like a car alarm going off nonstop. It's high-pitched, and it's all you can focus on.”

Basura has worked on other projects like making luxury wear for dogs and a partnership with Yerba Madre that made dirt shoes designed to break apart during a walk to spread wildflower seeds.

Along with Bezzy, the data centers project includes a collection of stickers that say things like “Every data center deserves a forever home” and “Open your heart. And your power grid.” Basu says the project is the result of dozens of interviews with people who live near data centers in the US. The website itself reads, “Adopt a data center: All they ask for is everything.”

Wilkis, whose band Big Data has “It’s giving Black Mirror, but make it music” in its Spotify description, says that the one upside of the data center debate is that the backlash is genuinely bipartisan.

“AI is a proxy for decades of widening wealth inequality in America, and data centers are its physical embodiment,” Wilkis wrote to WIRED. “With roughly 40 percent of the stock market's value riding on a handful of tech companies, the US economy is already a bet on AI's success.”

Sadly, only 20 Bezzy dolls are available for $99 from the Adopt a Data Center website and the Big Data storefront. Basura designed the toys, which are handmade in the US. But the physical toy isn’t the real point. The satire is meant to hook people into looking at the facts for themselves. When you click “adopt now” on the website, you’re taken to a statement with links to research and stories about how data centers fit into the world.

“It’s not about whether AI data centers should exist,” Basu says. “It’s about who gets to decide where they go, what resources they consume, and whether the communities living beside them actually benefit.”

entries.title: Meta’s Copyright System Is Being Weaponized Against Albanian Protesters
entries.summary: After three months of daily anti-government protests—dubbed the Flamingo Revolution—the sudden mass suspension of Instagram accounts has led to fears of brigading against demonstrators.
entries.content:
European lawmakers are calling for an investigation into Meta after the mass suspension of accounts posting about anti-government protests in Albania, in what observers believe is a coordinated brigading attack.

“What happened in Albania is tantamount to censorship,” said MEP Alexandra Geese in a statement. She is one of more than 30 Members of the European Parliament who signed a letter asking the European Commission to investigate whether Meta's actions complied with the EU's Digital Services Act.

“Mark Zuckerberg’s understanding of ‘freedom of speech’ only seems to cover opinions that align with the political agenda of the Trump administration. This is precisely why we have European rules,” she added.

The “Flamingo Revolution” protests, initially sparked by the development of a luxury resort linked to Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, have been taking place daily in the Albanian capital for over three months, demanding changes in the law that allows development on protected land as well as the resignation of the country’s prime minister. The Meta account suspensions almost all appear to be the result of copyright complaints and appear to have begun in late August.

An NGO group investigating the Meta suspensions alleges to WIRED it has evidence that “strongly indicates coordinated activity” led to the complaints.

“What quickly distinguished this from ordinary content moderation was the concentration of cases around the same political and civic movement,” said Martha Dimitratou, founder of Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organization that tracks digital censorship. In at least one case, the complaint was traced to someone who claimed they had been paid to make the complaint.

Dimitratou told WIRED they had verified around 100 cases of account restrictions connected to protests. “We continue to receive additional reports and, based on the volume and patterns we are seeing, estimate that the true number could be several hundred,” she says.

“We also identified that multiple posts on an account would receive copyright complaints, often five to 10 in a relatively short period, followed by escalating enforcement and, in some cases, the disabling of the entire account,” Dimitratou says. “Taken together, the alleged paid reporting, the repeated sequence of copyright complaints followed by account enforcement, the concentration of targets around the same movement, and the repeated targeting of replacement accounts strongly indicate coordinated activity,” Dimitratou added.

Repro Uncensored found that nearly all affected accounts appeared to be targeted with reports of copyright infringement. In at least 70 cases, the group confirmed removal of posts and videos about the protests, account restrictions, and loss of collaboration features.

“Collectively, the targeted accounts reach millions of people, meaning that when they are restricted or removed, millions can lose access to news, political information, protest documentation, and civic voices they rely on,” Dimitratou says.

One protester told WIRED that the person reporting his account said they had been paid to conduct the attack. On August 20, Arjan Koçi began receiving an influx of emails from Meta. “Someone was claiming that I had taken their work and published it as mine. But it was my video, my voice, my picture,” says Koçi, a British-Albanian who had been documenting the protest on his Instagram account since June.

Koçi’s aerial drone footage showed the massive scale of the demonstrations in Tirana and got millions of views across platforms. “If you receive too many of these reports, Meta will restrict your account,” he told WIRED. Around the same time, he said, several other protesters were also facing similar reports against their accounts. “It was about 1 o'clock in the morning, and I know at least 20 accounts that were closed at the same time,” he said.

“This tactic of mass copyright reporting, commonly called brigading, is an abuse of the systems that Meta has in place for people to report genuinely problematic, abusive, dangerous, or illegal content on their platforms,” said Kian Vesteinsson, deputy director for tech policy and digital rights research at Freedom House. “We've even seen this sort of brigading happen at scale in the context of a war or a conflict. Certainly, it's a tactic that we saw carried out by the Myanmar military, for example, to go after people criticizing the government's conduct,” he told WIRED.

Five of the reports made against Koçi’s content came from the same source with the same email address. He decided to reach out to the complainant. “I told him, ‘You have made a mistake; you are claiming my work as yours. Why are you doing this?’”

To his surprise, Koçi received a response. “He asked for my contact and then texted me.” The person told Koçi that he had been paid $1,800 to report these accounts and would withdraw his complaints if Koçi paid him. “He said he would accept crypto as payment.”

When Koçi refused, the person shared a piece of advice: “If you want to keep your account safe, deactivate it for a week.” Further attempts to contact the alleged attacker were met with silence. They did not respond to WIRED's attempts to contact them.

“Our research has found that copyright claims can trigger enforcement more readily than many other forms of reporting,” said Dimitratou, adding that often multiple complaints are deliberately directed at the same account, making them vulnerable to automated suspensions.

“The fundamental vulnerability is that a bad actor does not need to hack an account or directly prevent someone from publishing. They can weaponize the platform’s own enforcement infrastructure by falsely claiming ownership of material and repeatedly reporting,” Dimitratou said.

Vesteinsson told WIRED there was an additional vulnerability, in that “US-based platforms follow US copyright law. And specifically, the copyright framework set out under the DMCA, the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. And the DMCA has a notice-and-takedown provision that tends to favor overcompliance,” he said.

A Meta spokesperson told WIRED that the accounts were removed in error and have been restored, without commenting on the investigation. “We're sorry for the inconvenience caused. We have an appeals process for people to use when they think we've made a mistake, so we can restore content if we determine it doesn’t violate.”

The source of attacks remains unclear. Koci and others have accused the Albanian government of orchestrating attacks. “They want to close the protest down because this protest is one of the biggest protests in 35 years,” he said.

Albanian prime minister Edi Rama has rejected the accusations. “We have nothing whatsoever to do with any social media account being disabled or restricted, nor do we possess the technical capability to carry out an operation of this kind. Shame on this whole bunch of failures for spreading such nonsense,” he said on X. The prime minister's office did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.

While Koçi’s account has since been restored, he said he still believes he is shadow banned.

European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed in a press briefing that the commission is already investigating Meta over concerns relating to the shadow banning of political voices and said the latest allegations were “definitely not a surprise.” The commission confirmed that the investigation is ongoing and highlighted the role of the Digital Services Act in enabling users to challenge unjustified content moderation decisions.

entries.title: Best Gifts for Mom (2026): E-Readers, Digital Wall Calendar, Smart Bird Feeders
entries.summary: From a calendar that keeps my family organized to a frame that rescues photos from my camera roll, these favorites make thoughtful gifts.
entries.content:
Moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario. That includes Mother's Day, her birthday, Christmas, Hanukkah, or any other holiday in your family's life that includes gift-giving. The holiday season is right around the corner, and I've added a few gift ideas with that time of year in mind.

If you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love. From wellness gadgets that can improve her skin, the best tote bags I've tried, and even a device that puts her digital calendar in an IRL device, moms everywhere can get a ton out of these gifts. Many of these items I've given to my mother, or other WIRED staffers have given to theirs, or it's at the top of my list as a mother of a 4-year-old.

Updated September 2026: I've added two tote bag gift ideas for the fall season, the Wildbird Pregnancy Pillow as a gift for expecting moms, and more options in the gaming section.

Featured Gifts

Next-Level Skin (and Scalp) Care

The must-have gadget for women of almost any age is an LED mask. These masks promise to use red light to erase wrinkles, brighten your skin, and keep acne at bay. I haven't seen much change in my wrinkles in my year-plus of regularly using a red light mask, but I can confirm it makes my skin brighter and calms down acne and scars much faster when I'm regularly treating my skin. HigherDose is a favorite mask of mine because the three-strap design lets it hang on my head rather than squeeze it, making it one of the most comfortable masks I've worn.

My other favorite LED tool actually sits on my head and also comes from HigherDose. The brand's Red Light Hat treats your head with red light to rejuvenate your scalp and hair follicles for better hair growth, and as someone with a sensitive scalp and a hair-pulling problem, using this cap regularly genuinely improved my scalp and hair. It's the healthiest it's ever been, and my scalp is the least itchy, too. I love that this hat also has a battery pack, so I can comfortably wear it anywhere while I treat my head.

A Cool Tote

Look, nothing says mom life like looking for the perfect bag. I'm in a massive tote phase of my life; I somehow need to either lug an armload of items for myself and my son (or just myself!) or I only need a tiny belt bag. There's no in between.

The Yardsale Day Bag has been my go-to for a variety of needs, from a stylish personal item for a flight to a gym bag to the aerial studio. It's got a waterproof bottom that makes me happy to bring it to the zoo's splash pad, and a magnetic middle separator you can flex to separate the middle of the bag into two medium sections to better divide all your items. Plus, there are a handful of side pockets inside, but none are large enough for my massive Owala water bottle. I have the 30L in Butter, but there's also a smaller 20L version if you're looking for something a little more compact.

If your mom wants something a little more stylish, the Alex Mill totes are always on my mind. They come in a variety of gorgeous colors and are made of coated canvas, so they can put up with daily adventures, and you can customize them with your mom's initials (or even just the word “mom”!) with Alex Mill's hand-painted letter service. It's a simpler tote with no other pockets, but you can use the top snaps to let out the sides or tuck them in, depending on how much space Mom needs on a given day. The weathered color and vibe of these bags also feel perfect for the fall season.

Her Google Calendar IRL

My latest favorite family planning gadget is a digital wall calendar. These handy devices take the Google Calendar I live by (and just about any other digital calendar, if your mom isn't a Google girl) and put it on a physical device I can quickly tap into without needing to grab my phone or bark at Alexa. The Skylight Calendar 2 is my favorite, because it not only includes to-do lists, meal planning, and a recipe book but also doubles as a digital photo frame. That means it displays cute photos of my family most of the time, and then, with a simple tap, it opens the calendar or whatever page I was last on to show me what's on my family's schedule. It does have a subscription fee, though, to get the digital photo frame feature and a few other options, like meal planning. But I think it's well worth it to get so many features in a single device.

For the Expecting Mom

I'm expecting again, and this time I'm on a mission to find a good pregnancy pillow. I tried a large body pillow on the advice of another site for my first pregnancy, and it was honestly an awful experience—the pillow was too large and firm for me to comfortably use, let alone have room for both it and my growing midsection in my bed. Plus, it was heavy to move around, which is annoying when your body already feels too heavy to move around.

So far, the Wildbird Pregnancy Pillow has been the opposite experience. It's slim and light with just enough squish to add a little support under or around my belly without being difficult to get comfortable. It’s beautiful and easy to maneuver around. Wildbird also suggests it for other support positions postpartum, and I'm curious if those will work for me. But it makes for a beautiful gift for any expecting mom and will be one she's excited to put on her bed and curl up with at night.

Chic Sun Protection

I managed to get two different scalp burns in the first few weeks of summer, and I was seriously over it. My 4-year-old loves dragging me into sunny places, and even sunscreen made for spraying into the crevices of my hair hasn't kept me safe. This Solbari wide-brimmed hat is soft and flexible, so it's easy to fold up and store in a beach bag or stroller, and the cotton-linen design keeps it pretty breathable, though you'll want to reverse it to the white side for hotter days. It promises UPF 50+​ to protect your head, and the 4-inch brim helps keep my neck safe too. It's cute while still giving plenty of coverage and is a great pick for any mom who is going to be dragged into the sun all summer long.

For the Reader

Look, I love a Kindle, but if you want to get the best e-reader for your buck, the answer is actually a Kobo. My favorite is the Kobo Libra Colour that's cheaper than the Kindle Colorsoft and can also double as a digital notebook if you add on the $70 stylus. I also prefer Kobo's annotating options: You can write right on the pages instead of in weird pop-up margins and boxes only on Kindle. Kobo also has its own page-turner remote now, which I love to pair with a pillow stand holder so I can lean back and relax without holding up my e-reader while I read. I gave a similar pillow stand to my mom, and now I can spot her last reading spot easily because that pillow is resting there.

Luxurious, Cooling Sheets

If your mom (or your wife) is complaining about sleeping hot, one of the best kinds of sheets to keep her cool is a set of linen sheets. These beautiful sheets from Modern Dane are made of 100 percent European flax linen that's grown in France, Belgium, and the Netherlands and produced in Portugal. These sheets have a weight of 165 GSM, or grams per square meter, which is what linen sheets are graded on instead of thread count. That gives them a medium weight, but these sheets feel nice and light and have been perfect to sleep on during hot summer nights. Plus, these sheets are certified with Oeko-Tex Standard 100 Class 1 and Masters of Flax Fibre certifications. You can choose from a variety of colors and prints that will perfectly match her bedroom design.

Clear Listening

My husband and I got AirPods around the same time. We were late adopters and longtime fans of our Apple corded headphones. The AirPods 4 aren't the WIRED team's favorite for sound, but I'm one of the many people who can't seem to keep other earbuds in my ears, so Apple's tip-free design is the best fit for me. (Though that means you aren't getting good noise canceling, which is a big appeal for some parents!) If your mom complains that no earbuds seem to fit her, and she's an iPhone user, she might like these as much as I do.

I got my first set for Christmas from my siblings last year, and originally I stuck some pretty stickers on my case to tell the difference between my case and my husband's. I've since upgraded to this stylish case from Troubadour (previously Mujjo), which makes it easy to see which is mine and clip it onto my keys. It's a nice accessory if your mom already has AirPods but struggles to keep track of them or is looking for an easier way to differentiate hers from the other members of the house.

Gamer Gear

Once my kiddo is asleep, you can find me parked on the couch playing video games. I upgraded to a Nintendo Switch 2 ($449) earlier this summer so I could finally buy and play Pokopia ($70), since it's exclusive to the new console, and I already can't wait to use it to play the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time ($60) remake coming out in November. It's also quickly become an experience I can share with my son now that he's 4; he's been helping me and my husband replay Tears of the Kingdom, but he mostly requests we help him build monster-hunting robots and cook food for Link like he's a starving Tamagotchi.

If you're not looking to upgrade her console just yet but need a Switch-friendly cozy game for her, Stardew Valley has another big update in the works and only costs $15. I'm also hoping we see Fields of Mistria ($14) come to the Switch eventually, but the full launch came out in August for Steam users and has major quality-of-life improvements if she has played Stardew one time too many. My husband also upgraded his gaming setup this summer with a Steam Machine (from $1,049), and I have big plans to start using it often for Fields of Mistria. If your mom loves games, she'll love any one of these new devices or new games if she already got herself the new gadget like I did.

Photo Spotlight

As a mom, I take a lot of photos of my family. A lot. And sometimes it feels like all those great photos of my son's milestones go to my camera roll and photo storage to die. There are two solutions I love for this that are incredibly giftable: a digital photo frame she can instantly upload images to, and a printed photo book where you can take the best of the best and put them at her fingertips. I have and love both for different reasons. I love the digital photo frame to add all the photos from a fun weekend at the San Diego Zoo or Los Angeles Renaissance Pleasure Faire for me to relive again and again, but I also love being able to pull a photo book from the bookshelf and relive a specific moment I know is waiting there for me. Aura makes my favorite digital photo frames (followed by Skylight and the Calendar 2 if you want a multipurpose device, but Aura has no subscription fee if you only want photos), while Mixbook has been a favorite of mine for a while when it comes to printing photos, and has great starting prices for its photo books.

A Bird’s-Eye View

If you know a mom who loves to bird-watch (I know one!), you can upgrade her bird feeder to a smart one. Smart bird feeders add a camera to the feeder so she can see a close-up feed of the birds that come to hang out in her yard, and they're adorable to boot, for a little smart curb appeal. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck recommends the original Birdfy Lite as a great gift; it's her favorite smart bird feeder and comes in adorable colors to brighten your mom's yard and catch the eye of neighborhood birds. But the one she and I both have our eye on (her for her mother, me for myself) is the Birdfy Nest Duo, which is actually a birdhouse with two cameras so you can see the birds entering the nest outside and raising a family inside.

An Adorable Pan

I didn’t know I needed a tiny cast iron pan until it arrived. Field Co’s hand-finished, preseasoned cast iron pans are already known for being both lightweight and handsome. But with a mere 5-inch cook surface, this one might even cross the line from handsome into “cute.” But that’s what makes it a good gift: Your mother almost certainly does not have a cast-iron pan this small, and yet it also has real utility. At just 2 pounds, this pan is easy to pull out and stash, easy to maneuver or flip a pancake, easy to serve from, and the perfect size to fit the perimeter of a two-egg omelet. In addition to an egg pan, it’s a great, low-effort, single-serving pan in general—whether for grilled cheese, a little bit of bacon or sausage, or a couple of chicken thighs. The egg pan can be bought all by itself. But for $60 more, the gift set is nice. It comes with a cleaning kit (with maybe my favorite chain mail scrubber in existence), some seasoning oil, and a leather handle cover in cognac, black, brown, or cherry. —Matthew Korfhage

Compression Care

There's a wellness gadget for everything now. Rings that track your sleep and blood oxygen levels, masks to make you look younger, massagers to relax your muscles, and now boots to improve circulation. WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane says her mom loves these compression boots from Therabody to improve circulation, which is a common problem for many of our aging parents. These boots combine compression, vibration, and LED therapy into a single wearable device that comes with eight preset routines to focus on legs, knees, and joints. It's a unique option if she wants better recovery for her legs or better circulation for her health.

Better Espresso

The DeLonghi Rivelia is the best and easiest and most user-friendly superautomatic espresso machine I have tested. What’s superautomatic mean? It means you pour whole beans into the hopper, put milk in the milk carafe, and select the drink you want to make on the touchscreen menu. Then you let the machine do most of the rest. The style of espresso made by a superautomatic machine like this Rivelia is generally a bit smoother and less intense than the sort you get in a café. But the process is also less finicky; you won’t be dealing with coffee grounds and portafilters. What’s especially nice with this Rivelia is the ability to make multiple “profiles” for different coffee drinkers in the house, each with their own favorite drinks—and the ability to swap out bean hoppers to make decaf coffee in the afternoon. The Rivelia is also the machine my own mother, a drinker of lattes and dark-roast beans, loves unreservedly. Like others on the WIRED Reviews team, I often ask colleagues and those close to me to test my top-rated machines over long periods to see how they hold up over months or years of regular use. My mother thanks me nearly every month for letting her test the Rivelia. —Matthew Korfhage

For Ultimate Everything Showers

For most moms, showers are sacred—especially for moms of babies or younger kids. However, heavy metals, sediments, chlorine, and PFAS can cause health problems not just in drinking water, but in water that touches the skin, as well. They can also cause buildup on hair and shower surfaces, making them harder to clean. Many municipalities—including mine—treat water with chlorine, and when I asked him which filter he'd recommend for my own shower, WIRED water filter reviewer Matthew Korfhage suggested the Weddell Duo. It's the only US filter he's found that has certification for chlorine and lead removal from NSF International, and it also cites third-party testing by IAPMO R&T showing it can remove PFAS, though there's no corresponding certification. Still, the Duo has a 2.5-gallon-per-minute flow rate and can remove most chlorine from over 8,000 gallons' worth of showers. It's an in-line filter, so it's easy to install in minutes—just screw it in between your pipe and showerhead. It even comes with a little roll of waterproof tape to ensure a leak-free fit, and because of the horizontal orientation, installation won't affect the showerhead height. The filter needs to be replaced every three months, but refills only run about $25, compared with competitors like Filterbaby or Rorra, which can cost $40 to $45. —Kat Merck

entries.title: Submit Your Questions: Why Is Silicon Valley Still a Boy's Club?
entries.summary: How are women really faring in Silicon Valley? Submit your questions to our panel and we'll give you the scoop.
entries.content:
In 2026, as DEI and woke were declared over, WIRED set out to investigate the state of gender in Silicon Valley. As tech titans embraced Trump and the right, as Mark Zuckerberg declared that “masculine energy” was needed and Elon Musk cut federal female workers most of all, the backlash was in full swing. In our effort to understand the state of women in tech, we found frustrated females, confusion over who are the new AI girlbosses, and a total lack of interest in talking about gender at all.

Below this article, ask us all your burning questions about women in tech, which our panel will answer at our upcoming subscriber-only livestream on September 24 at noon ET / 9am PT. To leave questions for the panel, head to the comment section below.

  • Sandra Upson: a features editor at WIRED who brings to life some of our most ambitious, future-defining stories. Sandra will host the livestream.
  • Lauren Goode: a senior correspondent at WIRED covering all things Silicon Valley, including artificial intelligence, semiconductors, venture capital, startups, workplace culture, and tech's most interesting people and trends. She cowrites the Backchannel newsletter.
  • Ej Dickson: a senior culture writer at WIRED, focusing on internet culture. Read her recent feature on a college student who fought back against the burnerverse, a loosely connected online community of sports fans who dox and humiliate young women.

The event will be streamed right here. For subscribers who are not able to join, a replay of the livestream will be available after the event. Not a subscriber yet? Subscribe now to get access to this livestream, plus full access to WIRED.

In the meantime, check out past livestreams on all the essential features in ChatGPT, advice for getting started with Claude, and more.

entries.title: He Won the Nobel Prize for Protein Design. Now He Uses AI to Create Molecules Not Found in Nature
entries.summary: David Baker spoke with WIRED en Español about where biological design is headed next and the great potential and risks of taking biology outside the bounds of the natural world.
entries.content:
The natural world as we know it represents only a fraction of what might exist. Based on this idea, AI BioDesign was born: a scientific project that combines artificial intelligence and large-scale laboratory experiments to design and test new molecules and biological functions that are not found in nature but are physically and chemically possible.

In doing so, the researchers are aiming to create databases, models, and tools that could serve as “seeds” for developing the medicines and technologies of the future. The authors envision, for example, new drugs to treat cancer and neurodegenerative diseases or enzymes capable of breaking down plastics in the ocean.

The initiative is led by the Allen Institute, a biomedical research nonprofit in Seattle, along with the University of Washington and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center. Among the scientists leading the charge is David Baker, who shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work in computational protein design.

For much of the history of biology, scientists have studied the solutions forged by billions of years of evolution. Exploring possibilities that nature never produced is a fundamentally new approach. And as technology makes this now possible, one that a leaders of the field even compares the potential of these methods to historic transformations such as industrialization, electrification, and the digital revolution.

However, delving into completely novel regions of biology also inevitably leads to difficult questions. WIRED en Español spoke with David Baker, chief scientific officer at AI BioDesign, to address this and other topics.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

JORGE GARAY: AI BioDesign seeks to explore possible molecules and biological functions that have never existed in nature. Are there any particular risks involved in venturing into this uncharted territory? How can scientists anticipate those risks and what steps can they take to minimize them before a designed molecule leaves the lab?

DAVID BAKER: What’s exciting about biology is that nature has explored only a fraction of what is physically and chemically possible, which opens a world of possibilities for what we could design. When we explore those possibilities, the primary risks are not much different than those associated with any new biological technology—unintended interactions with living systems, unexpected environmental effects, or misuse.

The advantage we have today is that computational design allows us to evaluate many of these risks before a molecule is ever synthesized. We can screen designs computationally, test them extensively in contained laboratory settings, and subject them to increasingly realistic experimental validation before considering any real-world application.

The project mentions possibilities ranging from new drugs to plastic-degrading enzymes and even biological computers. If we have greater predictive power when designing new molecules and biological functions, how far do you think this capability could take us?

My team and I have lofty goals for protein design: We’re working to build a world where a cure for a new disease is created in weeks, not decades. Where our air, water, and soil are clean because we removed pollutants and reimagined the processes that contaminated them. Where crops thrive in conditions that once killed them. Where molecular machines pull critical minerals from waste and repair the infrastructure we depend on.

Proteins are the molecular machines life has developed to create all organic matter we know of here on Earth. Unlocking their full potential requires that we derive engineering principles that make it possible for innovative new ideas, including ones we can’t yet imagine, to be achievable.

As these models become more capable, could AI eventually design functional molecules that scientists themselves do not fully understand? If so, would it be enough to experimentally demonstrate that they work and are safe, or do you think we also need to understand the mechanisms?

Science has often progressed in stages, and we see that mirrored in how machine learning has advanced protein design. The first step is usually observing that something works, and we often only later understand why. Machine learning is really good at that first stage—it has vastly improved our capability to observe patterns that can be leveraged for biological design. Strong experimental evidence can justify moving forward with projects, but deeper understanding remains an important objective both for our research and scientific inquiry overall. Much of what we cannot achieve today is due to a lack of understanding or data that defines the parameters for how specific systems work or do not. This is the crux of the AI BioDesign program.

Are there molecules or biological functions that, in your opinion, should not be designed, even if it were technically possible to do so? What criteria should determine where that line is drawn?

Decisions should be guided by a balance of potential benefits and potential harms. Applications that address major challenges in health, sustainability, or human well-being have a strong case for development. Conversely, designs that create significant risks to public safety, security, or the environment deserve heightened scrutiny and, in some cases, clear restrictions.

Just as we have developed frameworks for other powerful technologies, we need governance structures that evolve alongside advances in AI and biotechnology. I’ve advocated that those restrictions should include monitoring and logging all synthetic DNA that is manufactured to record the sequence and its creator. This creates a practical barrier to misuse and a record of any ill-intentioned attempts.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: The Leftist Split Over AI Doom
entries.summary: The left wants AI regulation. They just can't agree on what it should look like or how concerned they should be.
entries.content:
On September 10, two days after researcher Jacob Coxon, who had recently quit his job at Anthropic, sounded the alarm about the industry potentially bringing about the end of humanity, the New York City Democratic Socialists of America posted a carousel of images on Instagram. The first slide was a drawing of an ouroboros—a dragon eating its own tail—set against a hot pink background. “AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story: both keep your attention on a science-fiction future to distract you from the real harms experienced in the present,” the image reads.

The post was authored by the NYC DSA’s Tech Action Working Group, which focuses on tech regulation issues for the chapter, the largest in the country. It garnered more than 25,000 likes on Instagram. But not everyone agreed with the post: “Horrible and dangerous take,” one comment reads. “Sometimes sounding the alarm is justified.”

As politicians scramble to understand AI safety, an ideological split is opening on the American left. Among the questions it’s centered on is whether to believe tech companies’ claims that their products are so powerful that they could end the world.

Some on the left question the value in elevating theoretical concerns about AI over actual harms. They believe repeating claims promoted by the frontier labs about the dangers of AI empowers the AI companies, turning attention away from regulating the current harms of the technology and toward an impossible future.

“AI has become the latest tool of capitalist exploitation. The damage that unregulated and misused AI is already causing is clear across the country,” Alan Dang, a member of Tech Action, tells WIRED. “As socialists, we don’t trust these corporations to craft their own regulations.”

But others are following the direction of Senator Bernie Sanders, the unofficial leader of the American left, who has enthusiastically taken up the AI safety issue, asserting that AI has the potential to eliminate humanity. They say that it’s possible to address all harms from AI—both those happening now and those that could happen in the future—at once.

“The same people concerned about frontier governance and the development of superintelligence are also addressing those current harms,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI issues. “We should address all these other important factors. Those frontier AI abilities are true and increasing in power. They are not fake or hype.”

Over the past year, Sanders dove head-first into the world of AI safety, bringing conversations that were previously happening in Bay Area circles to Washington and his large populist base. The 85-year-old was early to both opposing data centers—a massive organizing pole for the left this year—and speaking out about AI’s potential harms, from job loss to existential dangers. His data center moratorium bill, released in March, explicitly linked pausing construction with the need to pass federal regulation to protect “the future of humanity.”

Sanders’s positioning on this issue has put him in some unusual alliances, most notably with Steve Bannon, President Donald Trump’s former adviser and a right-wing populist podcast host. It has also seemingly inspired a raft of messaging from left-wing candidates running for office across the country, many of whom have been tying broader concerns around AI to the furor over data centers. On September 9, a day before the New York DSA post, six candidates affiliated with the Working Families Party, including four backed by Sanders, released statements on the need for Washington to regulate AI to prevent existential threats to humanity.

This has come with both public and private criticism. AI researcher and tech industry critic Timnit Gebru has accused Sanders and others on the left of “taking their cues from literal doomsday eugenicist cults,” referring to the effective altruist and rationalist philosophies, which underpin AI safety conversations in Silicon Valley. And Sanders’s moves have inspired some private agita within certain left-wing circles.

“Some of us are looking at Bernie and saying, what happened?” one NYC DSA member with a tech background tells WIRED.

Rumman Chowdhury, CEO and founder of the nonprofit Humane Intelligence, understands the concerns expressed by the DSA working group. Chowdhury, who formerly led the machine learning ethics, transparency, and accountability team at Twitter, thinks that all the attention that the AI safety discourse is generating will ultimately be beneficial to frontier labs.

“[The companies] grab all the attention, time, energy, and money by spouting really extreme perspectives. But then they actually backtrack to where we sit, all while they discount all of our expertise,” she says. “I think it's hard for normal people to think of how the mind of a venture capitalist works and these investors work. The scarier and more fantastic these CEOs make these companies seem, the more investors want in on it.”

For AI companies—particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, which aim to go public in the coming years—the attention and scrutiny on their products now could also be a boon in the long run. “Part of IPOing is sharing a lot of diligence documentation on risks and how risks have been addressed,” says Chowdhury. “This way, they can say, there is a full regulatory regime that they are part of establishing in this industry to guard against the worst risks, and that we have all established exactly what the ‘worst risks’ are.”

Pragathi Barusubramanian is a member of the NYC DSA’s Tech Action working group and a leader in the group’s anti-data center organizing, which netted a major win earlier this year by helping New York pass a one-year moratorium. Barusubramanian feels there may be a disconnect in the conversation around what exactly constitutes the most pressing AI-related harms to regulate. “When it comes down to what's happening on the ground,” they say, the conversation about existential risk “doesn’t come up at all.” Instead, they say, “there's an understanding that AI and data center companies don't have our interests at heart.”

McCoy, who is advising several Congressional candidates on AI, asserts that there is no real divide between actual leaders on the left on the issue. McCoy noted that several members of the DSA, including New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, have come out with recent statements about Coxon’s warnings and the Hugging Face hack.

McCoy says Gebru and similarly-minded critics are “marginal, unrepresentative, and also, frankly, picking an unnecessary distinction. It’s yes and. We should address harms like surveillance and Flock cameras, and other important factors. These do not come in any way at the expense of governing frontier AI capabilities.”

Phil Aroneanu, executive director of Irreplaceable, a left-leaning pro-AI safety organization, says that his time working as a climate activist has informed his approach to the AI regulation question. He believes that addressing both AI’s immediate and existing harms as well as future threats is both needed and possible. (McCoy helped found Irreplaceable with an initial seed fund from the Center for AI Safety.)

“This very similar intersection between the direct impact of fossil fuel extraction, people's homes getting flooded out because of climate-change-fueled storms, and then the broader movement focusing on the longer-term issue of risks and emissions,” he says.

Sanders and New York representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez don’t appear to be on the exact same page, either. While she cosponsored Sanders’ data center moratorium legislation, including the language around AI threatening humanity in her own House version of the bill, she has not participated in the high-profile AI safety discussions that he has been present for. While Sanders has called AI “the most transformational technology in the history of the world,” much of Ocasio-Cortez’s language around AI thus far has focused on data centers and the harms to jobs the technology could create, and worries that the industry is creating a bubble.

When asked by a reporter about AI safety last week, Ocasio-Cortez threaded a careful line, saying that “two things can be true at once,” noting AI “can be very dangerous when pursued without any guardrails,” and warning that “we could be seeing an economic bubble collide with a technological frontier.”

As the safety conversation quickly coalesces in Washington and in statehouses around the country, the ultimate question for the left is not whether to support AI regulation, but what regulations the movement should put its time and resources behind. Dang told WIRED that the DSA Tech Working Group supports “comprehensive AI and tech regulation at the federal, state, and city level, addressing frontier model regulation while also fighting back against the ways that corporate AI is already being used.”

A convention resolution currently before the DSA, meanwhile, proposes organizational support for Sanders and representative Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence altogether—hardly something the frontier labs would agree on. And any ideological concerns within the DSA itself may not matter too much when voters get a say. A Politico poll released Wednesday shows that two in three Americans think that there is at least some risk that AI could “destroy humanity.”

Barusubramanian says that, if nothing else, they’re “happy that everyone is talking about AI now.”

entries.title: Mophie’s Extendable MagSafe 3-in-1 Charging Stand Is 50 Percent Off
entries.summary: Charge your trio of Apple gadgets–iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods–with one of my favorite telescopic stands.
entries.content:
Charging all your gadgets is an unavoidable daily task, but wireless charging makes it easy. Mophie’s uniquely extendable stand is one of the best Apple 3-in-1 wireless chargers I have tested. And it’s available at a deep discount right now at half off (technically it’s 49 percent off). While this 3-in-1 stand has been discounted before, I’ve never seen it this low.

A 3-in-1 MagSafe charging stand is the best way to keep your desk or nightstand clutter-free but still charge your gadgets every day. This Mophie MagSafe 3-in-1 Charging Stand has a pad for regular AirPods or wireless earbuds on the weighted base and an Apple Watch charger branching off. But this stand also features a clever trick: You can adjust the height of the iPhone charging pad.

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Mophie

MagSafe 3-in-1 Extendable Wireless Charging Stand

Whether you have a low nightstand or work at a standing desk, this clever, compact stand enables you to keep your iPhone in your eye line. You can also turn your phone to landscape orientation for StandBy mode to use your iPhone as a bedside alarm clock. The 15-watt iPhone charger sits atop a telescoping pole that can extend from 7.5 to 16 inches. The pad can also tilt to your preferred angle. For content creators or folks making video calls, it can also serve as a tripod to help you film a quick video or take video calls.

The Mophie MagSafe 3-in-1 Charging Stand is both MFi and Qi-certified to provide up to 15 watts to your iPhone. It can also deliver 5 watts to your Apple Watch and 5 watts to your wireless charging AirPods case or other wireless earbuds. You get a 36-watt power supply and a 5-foot USB-C cable in the box.

If you have issues with the height of your iPhone, this is the 3-in-1 stand you need. Height adjustment is not a feature I’ve ever seen in another charger, but you can find plenty of fixed-height alternatives in my best MagSafe chargers guide.

entries.title: It Still Feels Like Summer in Parts of the US. Blame El Niño
entries.summary: Heat records are being shattered thanks to a boost from the natural climate pattern—and burning fossil fuels, of course.
entries.content:
A summer that started early across the US has no intention of quitting, even as the calendar turns to autumn.

The culprits? El Niño and climate change, which contributed to this summer’s record-breaking warmth and are delaying pumpkin spice season.

Forecasters with the US Climate Prediction Center continue to see increased odds for hotter-than-normal temperatures across much of the country through at least the end of September.

Computer models show a pronounced ridge pattern, an atmospheric arrangement that can lock in sustained spells of warmer-than-normal conditions. This setup will feature widespread unseasonable warmth throughout the country, a pattern consistent with a strong El Niño. The greatest odds of above-normal temperatures exist around the Upper Midwest and the Deep South. Some models suggest temperatures could run 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above normal for the latter half of September.

The blast of unseasonably warm air comes after the hottest summer in US history in a year in which tens of thousands of heat records have fallen across the US. That includes nearly 44,000 record daytime highs and more than 53,000 record-high overnight minimum temperatures recorded at weather stations across the country. Thousands more monthly and all-time heat records have fallen since the start of 2026. Over the same period of time, only about 21,500 low-temperature records fell, or around one cold record for every four heat records.

Many of the busted records date back more than a century. Salt Lake City hit 109 degrees Fahrenheit on July 12, for example, marking its hottest-ever temperature since records began in 1874. Washington, DC, tied its all-time warmest overnight low of 84 degrees Fahrenheit on July 3, where daily observations date back to 1871.

The heat hasn’t relented, despite the calendar turning to September. Even areas that typically escape countrywide heat waves have suffered. Much of Southern California endured excessive heat warnings during the second week of September as hot conditions and soupy air made Rodeo Drive feel more like Bourbon Street.

Why Has Fall Started So Hot?

Climate change is far and away the primary driver of the extreme heat baking the US. Rising average temperatures raise the baseline for extreme heat, making very hot days even steamier now than they would’ve been just a few decades ago.

That trend has been especially notable at night: Many communities across the country have also seen a precipitous increase in overnight temperatures during the warm months as both temperatures and mugginess increase. The lack of relief is what makes heat waves particularly deadly; without beneficial overnight cooling, heat stress becomes too much for many people to withstand.

A warmer climate is also altering upper-level patterns in a way that’s more favorable to extreme heat events. Strong centers of high pressure aloft force air to sink toward the ground. This air heats up as it compresses, combining with intense sunshine and dry soils to ratchet the heat well above normal. These ridges, often called heat domes, are more common in a warming world.

When Will the Heat End?

While overall highs for the remainder of September won’t be as extreme as they are in July, many areas will continue to endure summer-like heat.

El Niño is also lurking in the background. This pattern of warmer-than-normal waters in the Pacific Ocean affects weather patterns around the world.

We typically feel El Niño’s greatest effects during the cold months as these abnormally warm ocean temperatures alter the jet stream, which are responsible for weather patterns during the autumn and winter months.

This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be a record-setting event. Each El Niño is different, but the patterns during previous strong El Niños suggest that a vast swath of the US is in for overall warmer-than-normal temperatures through the fall and winter. In other words, we’re likely not done breaking heat records yet this year.
